<system-reminder>
## Swarm Mode

You are now in "agent swarm" mode. The user may send tasks that require a large number of parallel subagents.

## Workflow

You do not need to use TodoList to record this workflow.

1. First, you may need to do a small amount of exploratory work before deciding how to divide the task across subagents. You may not need subagents during this exploratory phase.

2. After exploring, if you are convinced no subagent is needed to complete the task, tell the user why and wait for further instructions; otherwise, continue with the appropriate delegation.

3. Once you have enough context, do not handle the main work yourself. Use AgentSwarm with a `prompt_template` containing the `{{item}}` placeholder and an `items` array for the requested or appropriate number of subagents, partitioning the problem so each item gives one subagent a distinct part of the work. Pass `subagent_type` when the whole swarm should use a non-default subagent profile.

## Coordination

- Give each subagent a distinct scope of work.
- Avoid duplicating work across subagents.
- Avoid assigning conflicting changes or responsibilities to different subagents.
- Remember that subagents have your full capabilities. Do not overload their prompts with excessive detail; only describe the necessary background and each subagent's specific task.
- Unless the user explicitly specifies a lower limit, do not try to conserve the number of agents. AgentSwarm supports up to 128 subagents and queues launches automatically, so decompose work as finely as possible while keeping subagent responsibilities non-conflicting; combine tasks only when they are genuinely inseparable. If the subagents only need to read, inspect, or report back without making changes, their scopes may overlap slightly.
</system-reminder>

You are an autonomous engineer. The repository at /workspace is at an earlier state of a real-world project.

`/workspace/requirements/` contains every requirement as a separate file. Each file describes one change request. Read them all, implement every one. Order does not matter, but some changes depend on others.



You are running as a long-horizon autonomous engineering agent at
`/workspace`. This task spans many files and requirements, and is expected
to take many iterations.

Read every requirement under `/workspace/requirements/` (and any other
explicit requirement list referenced by the task) and only finish once
every single one is addressed. Cherry-picking or partial fixes will lead
to failure.



## Optional planning artifact

If you believe the task is complex enough to benefit from a plan, you may
write `/workspace/agent_plans/plan.json` before making changes. This is
optional. If you create it, it must be a JSON object with `nodes` and
`edges`. Each node must have string `id` equal to a requirement slug from
`/workspace/requirements/`, may include `label` and `layer`, and each edge
must use string `from` and `to` that reference those ids.



## Git workflow (required)

`/workspace` is initialized as a git repo. After finishing the
implementation for ONE requirement:

  1. `cd /workspace`
  2. `git add -A`
  3. `git diff --cached > requirement_patches/<slug>.diff`
  4. `git commit -m "impl: <slug>"`

Where `<slug>` is the requirement filename without the `.yaml` extension.
The patch file MUST be non-empty for the requirement to count as complete.
Never write or `touch` an empty `.diff` file.

You may run `git log`, `git diff`, `git show` at any time to inspect what
prior work has done — only your own commits will be there; no reference
solution is accessible.

## Recommended workflow

1. Read the task carefully and survey `/workspace` so you understand the
   code you are changing.
2. As a development agent, when implementing a requirement you may write
   tests under `/workspace/agent_tests/` to safeguard correctness and
   future stability — write them if you think they help, otherwise skip.
3. Keep iterating until every requirement is implemented. Do not stop at a
   partial fix, a first passing check, or one successful edit.
4. Do not narrow the scope on your own. Missing a requirement is a task
   failure even if the changed tests pass.
5. You may revise the same files and rerun focused checks as many times as
   needed before finishing.
6. Your final summary must report requirement coverage counts, including at
   least the total number of requirements reviewed and how many were
   implemented and blocked.

title: Allow to parse JSON objects into Strings in JSON input formats
category: other
requirement: '## Context

  A data engineer ingesting JSON into a `String` column may receive payloads where some fields are plain strings and others are nested JSON objects. Today those object values are rejected or coerced inconsistently, which makes mixed-shape feeds awkward to load even when the downstream requirement is simply to preserve the original JSON text.


  ## Desired outcome

  When the input format setting `input_format_json_read_objects_as_strings` is enabled, JSON input formats should accept object values for `String` targets and store the object as its JSON string representation instead of rejecting it. This should work both when parsing directly into declared `String` columns and when inferring types from JSON input that mixes strings with objects or maps.


  ## Acceptance signals

  With `input_format_json_read_objects_as_strings = 1`, a field containing `{...}` can be loaded into a `String` column and remains readable as serialized JSON text, while the default behavior stays unchanged when the setting is off. The new setting is documented and wired through format settings so users can reliably turn it on anywhere JSON input parsing is used.'

title: Add support of Date32 arguments for date_diff function
category: feature
requirement: '## Context

  A ClickHouse analyst using `dateDiff` or `date_diff` expects the function to work across the full supported date family, including historical dates stored as `Date32` and timestamp ranges that cross the Unix epoch.

  ## Desired outcome

  `dateDiff` must accept `Date32` anywhere users can already pass `Date`, `DateTime`, or `DateTime64`, including mixed-type combinations and const or materialized columns. The function also needs to return stable results for pre-1970 to post-1970 comparisons instead of relying on relative-number conversions that overflow or drift around the epoch boundary.

  ## Acceptance signals

  Queries such as `dateDiff(''hour'', toDate32(''1900-01-01''), toDate32(''1900-01-02''))` return `24`, mixed `Date32`/`DateTime64` combinations work in either argument order, and epoch-crossing calculations like `date_diff(''year'', toDate32(''1969-12-25''), toDate32(''1970-01-05''))` produce the documented results instead of failing or miscounting.

  '

title: Analyzer aggregate function lambda crash fix
category: bugfix
requirement: '## Context

  A ClickHouse user experimenting with the new analyzer can write expressions where lambda syntax is attached to an aggregate or window function. Today that path can reach unresolved function nodes and end in an internal exception instead of a clear user-facing rejection.


  ## Desired outcome

  If a lambda is supplied to a function that does not support lambda arguments, analysis should fail deterministically with a clear exception rather than a logical error or unresolved-node failure. In particular, aggregate and window functions must reject lambda arguments explicitly, and unresolved function nodes should report that the function node with that name is not resolved.


  ## Acceptance signals

  Queries that misuse lambda arguments on aggregate or window functions raise `UNSUPPORTED_METHOD` with messages such as `Aggregate function ''...'' does not support lambda arguments` or `Window function ''...'' does not support lambda arguments`, instead of crashing in analysis. Other argument-validation messages in the analyzer continue to reference the quoted function name consistently.'
title: Analyzer CTE resolution fix
category: bugfix
requirement: '## Context

  Analysts using common table expressions inside nested queries expect each reference to resolve in the correct scope, but the analyzer can currently bind a CTE incorrectly when it appears under a subquery boundary.


  ## Desired outcome

  Fix CTE resolution in the analyzer so nested and subquery-local references resolve to the intended `WITH` definition.


  ## Acceptance signals

  Queries that use CTEs inside subqueries analyze and execute correctly, without unresolved references or accidental binding to the wrong scope.

  '
title: Analyzer improve JOIN with constants
category: other
requirement: '## Context

  The analyzer has trouble with `JOIN` conditions that include constant expressions alongside the real join predicates. Users can write valid SQL that should be planned correctly but currently gets mishandled.


  ## Desired outcome

  `JOIN` analysis should tolerate constant terms in the `ON` clause without corrupting the join-condition handling or changing the intended semantics.


  ## Acceptance signals

  The affected `JOIN` forms with constants are analyzed successfully, and constant expressions in the `ON` clause no longer cause the planner to reject or mis-handle otherwise valid queries.

  '
title: Analyzer AST key condition crash fix
category: bugfix
requirement: '## Context

  The analyzer can fail on a specific AST key-condition pattern that users can reach with valid SQL. Instead of planning the query or rejecting it cleanly, the server hits an internal exception.


  ## Desired outcome

  The analyzer should handle that key-condition form robustly so users can run the query pattern without tripping an internal failure.


  ## Acceptance signals

  The previously failing key-condition query no longer raises the internal exception, and the analyzer produces a normal plan or a regular user-facing error if the query is invalid for some other reason.

  '
title: Minor fixes in annoy index documentation
category: bugfix
requirement: '## Context

  Analysts experimenting with approximate nearest-neighbor search need the Annoy index documentation to describe the feature correctly, because most users discover its limits and syntax from the docs rather than from the source.


  ## Desired outcome

  Tighten the Annoy index documentation so the guidance, terminology, and examples match the actual feature and do not create false expectations about how the index should be configured or used.


  ## Acceptance signals

  A reader can use the page as a trustworthy reference for Annoy indexes without running into contradictions, ambiguous wording, or examples that do not reflect real behavior.

  '

7

12

2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  An analyst using `singleValueOrNull`, `min`, `max`, or related single-result aggregates expects empty-input behavior to stay consistent instead of silently turning into a non-null value after internal state merges. 1	title: Improve referential dependencies
2	category: ci
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  A ClickHouse operator restoring backups expects dependent objects to come back in a valid order, especially when databases, tables, views, dictionaries, users, roles, settings profiles, and `ON CLUSTER` objects reference one another. Today referential dependencies are incomplete enough that restore order can be wrong, causing restore failures even though the backup itself is valid.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Backup restore should build a more complete dependency graph so referenced objects are restored only after the objects they depend on are available. This includes database and table references embedded in DDL, cluster-aware objects, and other named entities such as users, roles, and settings profiles that participate in restore ordering.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  End-to-end restore scenarios can create and back up objects such as `test.table`, users like `u1`, roles like `r1` and `r2`, and settings profiles like `prof1`, then drop them and restore them without dependency-order failures. Restores on a cluster also succeed when tables are created and recovered with `ON CLUSTER ''cluster''` or `ON CLUSTER ''cluster3''`, confirming that the dependency graph now captures those referential links.'

1	title: Implement backup to S3
2	category: feature
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  A ClickHouse operator needs to keep table backups in object storage rather than only local destinations, and the backup workflow should work the same way whether the S3 target is written directly in SQL or referenced through a named collection.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  `BACKUP ... TO S3(''endpoint/path'', ''key'', ''secret'')` and `RESTORE ... FROM S3(''endpoint/path'', ''key'', ''secret'')` should be supported, and the same workflow should also work with `S3(named_collection_s3_backups, ''backup_name'')` so teams can restore from S3 without embedding credentials in every statement.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  A table can be backed up to S3 and restored from the same backup location with normal `BACKUP` and `RESTORE` semantics, and environments that can use server-side copying continue to report that native copy is being used.
16	
17	  '

1	title: Fix locking while writing backup in multiple threads
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Users creating backups with multiple worker threads expect direct file-copy paths to benefit from concurrency rather than being serialized behind an unnecessary global lock.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Backup writing should only hold the global lock where correctness actually requires it, such as archive writes, while regular multi-threaded file writes and native-copy paths can proceed concurrently.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Non-archive backup writes no longer block each other unnecessarily, archive writes remain serialized for correctness, and the file-count bookkeeping stays thread-safe.
16	
17	  '

1	title: Fix reusing of files > 4GB from base backup
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  A ClickHouse operator using incremental backups with `SETTINGS base_backup = ...` expects unchanged files to be reused even when a single column file is larger than 4 GiB.
6	
7	  ## Desired outcome
8	
9	  Backups should identify those large files as reusable content instead of duplicating them or treating them as overflowed sizes.
10	
11	  ## Acceptance signals
12	
13	  An incremental backup of an unchanged part with a 4 GiB+ data file can be created and restored successfully, and the incremental backup stores only the backup metadata when no data file actually changed.
14	
15	  '

1	title: fix bandwidth throttlers initialization order
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Operators who configure global network bandwidth limits expect those throttles to apply predictably, but the current initialization order can leave the all-users throttler in the wrong state before per-user throttling is derived from it. That creates confusing traffic-control behavior.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Initialize bandwidth throttlers in the correct order so global and per-user limits are both built from a valid shared configuration.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  `max_network_bandwidth_for_all_users` is established before the dependent user throttlers are created, and the configured network limits behave consistently after startup.
16	
17	  '

1	title: full example using AggregatingMergeTree
2	category: other
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Users learning `AggregatingMergeTree` often struggle to turn the individual documentation fragments into a complete working example. The existing docs do not show the full flow clearly enough for someone trying to reproduce it.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Provide a fuller end-to-end example that demonstrates how a real `AggregatingMergeTree` workflow is meant to be set up and queried.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  The documentation includes a complete example sequence rather than isolated fragments, and a reader can follow it to understand the intended `AggregatingMergeTree` usage pattern.
16	
17	  '

1	title: minor fix error msg, replace outdated func name
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  When aggregation merge preparation receives no data at all, developers and operators rely on the exception text to identify the failing code path quickly. An outdated method name in that message makes debugging harder because the exception points to the wrong function.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  The empty-input exception in the aggregator should name `Aggregator::prepareVariantsToMerge` instead of the older `Aggregator::mergeAndConvertToBlocks`, while keeping the same failure condition and error code. This is a diagnostics fix only.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  If aggregation merge preparation is invoked with no variants, ClickHouse still throws `EMPTY_DATA_PASSED`, but the message now correctly says `Empty data passed to Aggregator::prepareVariantsToMerge.` so logs and error reports identify the real failing routine.
16	
17	  '

2	category: feature

11

13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Queries that compare aggregate states with complex nested types produce the expected result instead of failing on an incorrect cast, and existing aggregate-state comparison behavior stays intact for simpler types.
16	
17	  '

1	title: Analyzer subquery in JOIN TREE with aggregation
2	category: other
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Analysts can place a subquery with aggregation directly in the `JOIN` tree, and they expect the analyzer to accept that valid SQL instead of rejecting it as though aggregate functions appeared illegally in a plain join expression. The current analyzer also risks applying extra pruning logic in places where its syntax analysis is not yet ready.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  When the `JOIN` tree node is itself a subquery or `UNION`, the analyzer should permit aggregates, grouping functions, and window functions inside that subquery while still rejecting them in ordinary join expressions. At the same time, analyzer mode should avoid using the legacy partition-pruning path until the analyzer can supply the correct equivalent information.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Queries that join against aggregated subqueries stop failing with the old analyzer validation, non-subquery join expressions are still checked as before, and analyzer-enabled execution does not run the legacy partition-pruning branch that is known to be incompatible with the new analysis flow.
16	
17	  '

1	title: Fix  join to subqueries rewriter null pointer
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Analysts expect the join-to-subquery rewrite to handle aliases robustly, even when an alias expression is not itself a simple identifier. Today the rewrite can dereference a null pointer while trying to restore table qualification on such aliases, turning a valid query into an internal failure.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Alias normalization inside the join-to-subquery rewrite should only apply identifier-specific logic when the cloned alias is actually an `ASTIdentifier`. Non-identifier aliases must be handled safely so the rewrite either proceeds correctly or raises the intended ambiguity error instead of failing internally.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Queries that use non-identifier aliases in this rewrite path no longer hit a null-pointer failure, identifier aliases still receive the qualified-name clash check, and ambiguous qualified aliases continue to raise `AMBIGUOUS_COLUMN_NAME` when that is the real problem.
16	
17	  '

1	title: Fix assert cast in join on falsy condition
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  A ClickHouse user can write a `JOIN` whose condition simplifies to a falsy value, and that edge case should be handled as an ordinary query case rather than triggering an internal assertion path.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  `JOIN` planning and execution should handle falsy join conditions safely, preserving normal query semantics and returning a regular exception only when there is a genuine user-facing problem.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Queries with falsy join conditions no longer hit internal assertion-style failures during cast handling, and the resulting behavior is stable and predictable for the user.
16	
17	  '

1	title: 'Fix typos in JSON formats after #40910'
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: 'JSON row-output formats should write to the active output stream consistently after the recent refactoring in this area. `JSONEachRow` and `JSONCompactEachRow` must again emit valid delimiters, row wrappers, and serialized field values in all normal modes, including array-of-rows output, instead of sending pieces of the response to the wrong buffer. The outcome should be correct JSON text on the wire, not malformed or partially missing output.
4	
5	  '

1	title: Do not assume that the original query was valid when transforming JOINs
2	category: other
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  When a user writes an invalid multi-`JOIN` query, they need ClickHouse to report the original problem rather than quietly rewriting it into a different query that references some other table''s column.
6	
7	  ## Desired outcome
8	
9	  Join transformation should run only after the original query has been validated, so missing or invalid column references stay visible as user errors.
10

13	  Malformed join queries now raise the proper column-resolution exception even when join-to-subquery optimization would otherwise have rewritten them.
14

5	  Operators may encounter corrupted or maliciously malformed compressed data, and ClickHouse must reject that input safely instead of writing past the output buffer during LZ4 decompression. 2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Operators using `KeeperMap` can hit intermittent failures when a table is being dropped or created concurrently on different servers. Instead of retrying cleanly, ClickHouse can mis-handle disappearing metadata nodes or race with another server that created the same table path first.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9

11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals

15	  Concurrent `KeeperMap` create/drop activity no longer leaves operators with fragile race-dependent failures for normal retryable cases. Genuine conflicts still surface as explicit exceptions, while transient `ZNONODE` and `ZNODEEXISTS` races are treated as recoverable.

17	  '

2	category: other
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  A ClickHouse user filtering data in `PREWHERE` with 128-bit or 256-bit integer values expects those comparisons to be evaluated correctly, just like native-width integer filters.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  `PREWHERE` should correctly handle `(U)Int128` and `(U)Int256` values instead of misprocessing those non-native integer types during filter evaluation.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Queries that use `Int128`, `UInt128`, `Int256`, or `UInt256` values in `PREWHERE` return correct filtered results and no longer hit the old type-handling bug.
16	
17	  '

1	title: Hold ProcessListEntry a bit longer in case of exception from Interpreter
2	category: other
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  When an interpreter throws while a query is being set up or executed, operators and surrounding infrastructure still need the query''s process-list entry to remain valid long enough for orderly cleanup and inspection.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Hold the `ProcessListEntry` through the exceptional path so interpreter failures do not race with process-list lifetime management.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  The exception path no longer trips lifetime-related flakes or invalid access around process-list bookkeeping, and failed queries still clean up predictably.
16	
17	  '

1	title: Extend processors_profile_log with more info
2	category: other
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Operators diagnosing slow or memory-heavy queries from `system.processors_profile_log` can see timing data today, but they still cannot tell which plan step a processor belongs to or how many rows and bytes moved through it.
6	
7	  ## Desired outcome
8	
9	  Each processor profile record should expose both plan-grouping information and data-volume counters so query-plan analysis can identify where rows and bytes are entering and leaving a processor.
10	
11	  ## Acceptance signals
12	
13	  `system.processors_profile_log` includes `plan_step`, `plan_group`, `input_rows`, `input_bytes`, `output_rows`, and `output_bytes`, and those fields contain meaningful values for logged processors.
14	
15	  '

1	title: Every profile event must have documentation
2	category: docs
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Profile events are part of the operator-facing observability surface, so blank descriptions in `system.events` make those counters much harder to interpret during troubleshooting.
6	
7	  ## Desired outcome
8	
9	  Every profile event should expose a useful description, and that expectation should be enforced even for zero-valued events that only appear when zero values are requested.
10	
11	  ## Acceptance signals
12	
13	  With `system_events_show_zero_values = true`, `SELECT event FROM system.events WHERE length(description) < 10` must return no rows, including for cache, buffer, replication, and ZooKeeper-related events that previously lacked descriptions.
14	
15	  '

1	title: Fix `LOGICAL_ERROR` if fetch of projection was stopped
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  An operator using zero-copy replication with projections expects a cancelled or interrupted fetch to clean up safely instead of leaving broken partial state behind. Today, if fetching a projection stops midway, ClickHouse can throw a `LOGICAL_ERROR` during cleanup because projection files and transaction state are not rolled back consistently.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  If downloading a replicated part or any of its projections is interrupted, ClickHouse should clean up the partially fetched files and commit the cleanup transaction without raising a secondary internal error. The failure should remain a normal fetch interruption, not escalate into a misleading `LOGICAL_ERROR` about projection handling.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  The zero-copy projection cancellation scenario in replicated MergeTree no longer reports the previous `LOGICAL_ERROR`; instead the partial base part or `.proj` data is removed through the proper cleanup path. Operators can still rely on the fetch failing when interrupted, but not on lingering broken state afterward.'

1	title: Fix quota_key
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Operators and client applications rely on `quota_key` to make sure requests are charged against the intended quota, including pooled connections and secondary client utilities. At the moment, some connection paths can lose that value during setup, so quota enforcement does not always reflect the caller’s identity.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  `quota_key` should be transmitted reliably as part of connection establishment everywhere the native protocol supports it, so all relevant ClickHouse clients apply the same quota identity from the start of the session.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Connections that specify `quota_key` have it honored on first connect as well as through connection pools and auxiliary client paths, compatibility is preserved for peers that do not support the addendum, and quota-based accounting no longer depends on which client wrapper initiated the session.
16	
17	  '

1	title: Rename canonicalRand to randCanonical
2	category: refactor
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  SQL users need the canonical floating-point random function to follow ClickHouse naming conventions before it becomes part of a released public surface.
6	
7	  ## Desired outcome
8	
9	  Expose this function as `randCanonical` consistently in SQL, documentation, and examples, and do not keep the unpublished `canonicalRand` name as the public contract.
10	
11	  ## Acceptance signals
12	
13	  Users call `randCanonical` in queries and docs, and the function name matches the rest of the `rand*` family.
14	
15	  '

2	category: feature
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  A ClickHouse user doing simulation, sampling, or synthetic-data generation needs built-in SQL functions for drawing random values from common probability distributions instead of hand-rolling approximations outside the database.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  ClickHouse should provide distribution-aware random generators named `randUniform`, `randNormal`, `randLogNormal`, `randExponential`, `randChiSquared`, `randStudentT`, `randFisherF`, `randBernoulli`, `randBinomial`, `randNegativeBinomial`, and `randPoisson` so analysts can generate representative random data directly in queries.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Each function is callable from SQL with the expected distribution parameters, returns values of the appropriate shape for that distribution, and can be used in normal query expressions without extra setup.

17	  '

title: Fix drop of completely dropped table
category: bugfix
requirement: '## Context

  A ClickHouse operator dropping a replicated MergeTree table can reach a final cleanup stage after the table metadata has already disappeared from ZooKeeper.

  ## Desired outcome

  That shutdown path should treat an already removed table as a legitimate terminal state instead of recreating shared identifiers or failing local cleanup because the metadata is gone.

  ## Acceptance signals

1	title: Faster build
2	category: other
3	requirement: 'ClickHouse maintainers should not have to wait minutes for a single large quantile implementation unit to compile when they touch aggregate-function code. The quantile family should build from smaller translation units so developer build time improves while the registered quantile functions and SQL behavior remain unchanged. This is a build-performance improvement rather than a runtime query-speed change.
4	
5	  '

1	title: Fix undefined behavior in `quantiles` function
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Analysts expect `quantile*` functions to stay numerically safe even when the input stream contains `NaN` values or sanitizer builds exercise edge cases in the reservoir sampler. At the moment the sampling code can hit undefined behavior in those paths, which turns a normal aggregate query into a sanitizer failure instead of a stable result.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  The `quantile` family should handle `NaN` and similar edge-case inputs without undefined behavior in either the ordinary or deterministic reservoir samplers. Users should keep getting a valid aggregate result or the existing documented semantics, but never a sanitizer-only failure caused by the implementation itself.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Queries that aggregate values including `NaN` complete cleanly under UBSan and MSan, and both the standard and deterministic quantile sampler implementations follow the same safe update rules. No new function names or SQL syntax are introduced; this is correctness hardening for existing `quantile*` behavior.'

1	title: Fix rare possible hung on query cancellation
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Users expect `KILL QUERY` or other cancellation paths to stop work promptly, even if the execution graph is still expanding and adding processors at the same time. In a rare race, newly created processors can slip in after cancellation and leave a query hanging instead of stopping cleanly.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Once query cancellation starts, the execution graph should remember that it has been cancelled and refuse to add newly expanded processors into the live processor list. Any processors created after that point should be cancelled immediately so the query can finish shutting down rather than hanging.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Calling `cancel` marks the graph as cancelled, processors already registered are cancelled as before, and any later `expandPipeline` attempt stops by cancelling the newly created processors instead of attaching them to a query that is already being torn down.
16	
17	  '

2	category: other
3	requirement: '## Context
4

7

10	  The affected query-plan and pipeline types should use the new internal names consistently while preserving all existing runtime behavior, public SQL semantics, and operator-visible messages. Users should notice no difference beyond cleaner internal code organization.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals

15	  The codebase builds with the renamed internal symbols, and query execution behavior remains byte-for-byte compatible from the user’s perspective.'

1	title: Fix double escaping in the metadata of FORMAT JSON
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Consumers of `FORMAT JSON` metadata rely on the `meta` section to describe columns exactly once, and double-escaping field names makes valid identifiers look corrupted to downstream JSON readers.
6	
7	  ## Desired outcome
8	
9	  Emit pre-escaped column names in JSON metadata without escaping them a second time, so the `meta` section remains valid JSON and preserves the intended field names.
10	
11	  ## Acceptance signals
12	
13	  Column names that contain quotes or backslashes appear correctly once-escaped in `FORMAT JSON` metadata instead of being double-escaped.
14	
15	  '

1	title: Block memory tracker in Keeper during commit
2	category: other
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Operators running ClickHouse Keeper under write load need commit processing to be robust even when memory accounting is active. Internal bookkeeping during commit should not trigger avoidable memory-tracker interference that surfaces as operational instability.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Keeper should block or isolate memory tracking during the sensitive commit path so ordinary commit processing does not fail because of internal accounting noise.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Commit-heavy Keeper workloads continue to behave the same from a client perspective, but the affected commit path no longer reports spurious memory-tracker-related failures.
16	
17	  '

1	title: One more validation for broken config in keeper
2	category: other
3	requirement: 'A ClickHouse Keeper operator needs startup validation to reject broken RAFT server definitions before the service comes online. Configurations with duplicate server ids, duplicate hostname-port endpoints, localhost entries mixed with remote hosts when hostname validation is enabled, or repeated `<id>`, `<hostname>`, or `<port>` tags inside a single `<server>` block should fail fast instead of being partially accepted. At the same time, a valid Keeper configuration must still start normally and allow a simple `SELECT 1` health check to succeed.
4	
5	  '

1	title: Faster commit in Keeper
2	category: other
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Keeper throughput is heavily influenced by how much bookkeeping happens while a transaction commit is being finalized. Clearing too much cached node state at commit time adds avoidable overhead, especially when many nodes were touched but only a subset actually became stable at that zxid.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Keeper should make commit processing cheaper by only revisiting cached nodes whose paths have no further modifications in the current transaction, instead of scanning and clearing unrelated cache entries wholesale. This must preserve correctness of the node cache while reducing commit-time work.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  During `commit`, Keeper tracks only the paths that stop changing at the committed zxid, removes cached entries for those paths when appropriate, and avoids the broader cache sweep that previously made commit processing slower under write-heavy workloads.
16	
17	  '

1	title: 'Keeper fix: throw when port already in use'
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  A Keeper operator starting a node on a port that is already occupied needs an immediate and explicit startup failure, because silently continuing without the interserver listener leaves the node half-started and hard to diagnose.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Fail fast when the interserver listener cannot bind, and surface the exact startup problem with the message `Cannot create interserver listener on port {}`.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Keeper startup stops instead of limping forward when the port is already in use, and operators see the explicit `Cannot create interserver listener on port {}` exception in logs or startup output.
16	
17	  '

=== replicated-table-shared-id ===
title: Fix lost table shared id
category: bugfix
requirement: 'A replicated MergeTree table that was only partially initialized should still recover cleanly instead of losing its shared table identifier forever. If a replica asks for the shared id and finds it still unset locally, ClickHouse should safely recreate or load that id from ZooKeeper under proper synchronization and continue initialization. The desired outcome is that table startup and recovery are resilient to this interrupted-initialization case rather than failing on a missing shared id.

  '
=== replicated-worker-race ===
title: Fix benign race in database replicated worker
category: bugfix
requirement: '## Context

  Operators waiting for replicated databases to catch up need the worker coordination path to be concurrency-safe even under heavy background activity.


  ## Desired outcome

  The replicated database worker should stop relying on a race-prone logging/state access pattern while waiting for all entries to be processed. The observable behavior should stay the same except for removing the concurrency hazard.


  ## Acceptance signals

  The wait-for-processing path remains stable under concurrent worker activity, and the fix does not introduce any new user-visible behavior changes beyond removing the race.

  '
=== replicatedmergetree-coordination-races ===
title: Some fixes for ReplicatedMergeTree
category: bugfix
requirement: '## Context

  ReplicatedMergeTree operators need replication and ZooKeeper coordination to stay correct under heavy concurrency, because subtle races there can lead to stuck queues, inconsistent ephemeral locks, or hard-to-reproduce replication failures. This patch is about tightening that internal coordination rather than introducing a new SQL feature.


  ## Desired outcome

  Harden ReplicatedMergeTree''s coordination paths so ephemeral-lock handling, replication queue work, and related race-prone transitions behave deterministically even under injected scheduling noise. Existing replication semantics should remain the same from the operator''s perspective, but the implementation must be more resilient to concurrency edge cases.


  ## Acceptance signals

  Replication workflows that previously depended on lucky thread timing no longer fail or hang in the affected race windows, ZooKeeper-related coordination remains consistent during those transitions, and operators see the same external replication behavior with fewer intermittent internal failures.

  '
=== replicatedmergetree-shared-idempotency ===
title: Don't throw if shared ID already created in `StorageReplicatedMergeTree`
category: other
requirement: '## Context

  Operators running replicated `MergeTree` tables with zero-copy style workflows can attach or initialize replicas in the background while shared metadata already exists.

  ## Desired outcome

  `StorageReplicatedMergeTree` should treat an already-created shared ID as an idempotent condition during attach or startup instead of surfacing an unnecessary failure.

  ## Acceptance signals

  A replica can finish attach or startup when the shared ID is already present, and the table becomes available without requiring manual cleanup of that metadata.

  '

content.text:
You are one of many autonomous engineers working concurrently in the same git repository at /workspace — a ClickHouse source tree pinned at an earlier state. Each file /workspace/requirements/<slug>.yaml describes one change request (title, category, requirement with Context / Desired outcome / Acceptance signals).

Your assigned requirement slugs (implement ALL of them, in this order):
x-clickhouse-summary-mv-stats, xml-helper-consistency, yaml-to-xml-conversion, zero-copy-cleanup-safety, zero-copy-warning-docs

For EACH slug, in order:
1. Read /workspace/requirements/<slug>.yaml fully.
2. Explore the relevant code/docs/tests with Read/Grep/Glob to understand the current state. Many requirements correspond to real upstream ClickHouse changes from late 2022 — implement the equivalent change, minimally, matching surrounding code style.
3. Implement the change: source code, docs, tests, CI scripts — whatever the requirement actually asks for. Keep the diff focused; no drive-by refactors. If you add a stateless test, add both the .sql and .reference file and make them consistent with your implementation.
4. Verify as best you can WITHOUT building the whole project (a full ClickHouse build is infeasible). Use targeted checks: re-read your edits, grep for callers you may have missed, run python -m py_compile / bash -n for scripts you touched, etc.
5. Commit IMMEDIATELY after finishing this one requirement, before starting the next:
   cd /workspace
   git add <explicit list of only the files you changed for THIS requirement>
   git diff --cached > requirement_patches/<slug>.diff
   test -s requirement_patches/<slug>.diff || echo "ERROR: empty patch for <slug> — fix before continuing"
   git commit -m "impl: <slug>"
   If git fails due to index.lock (another agent is committing), wait a few seconds and retry. NEVER create or leave an empty .diff file.

CRITICAL concurrency rules:
- Other agents are editing and committing in the same repo RIGHT NOW. NEVER use `git add -A` or `git add .` — stage only the exact files you changed for the current requirement.
- Do not stage or commit: requirement_patches/ itself (other agents' diffs), tests/queries/0_stateless/02458_datediff_date32.sql (belongs to slug date-diff-date32 — if that's not in your list, don't touch it), __pycache__/, or any file you didn't intentionally modify for the current slug.
- Never run git reset/rebase/push/checkout -- or otherwise revert workspace changes that aren't yours.
- If a requirement appears already satisfied in the current tree, double-check carefully (the tree is at an EARLIER state — most things are genuinely missing). If after real investigation it is truly already done, you may make the smallest meaningful alignment change the requirement text supports; if there is honestly nothing to change, skip it and report it as blocked/already-done — do NOT commit an empty diff.
- Do not create documentation/summary .md files beyond what the requirement asks for.

When done with all 5, reply with a per-slug list: IMPLEMENTED (files touched) or BLOCKED (reason).

563	    void addBatchLookupTable8(
564	        size_t row_begin,
565	        size_t row_end,
566	        AggregateDataPtr * map,
567	        size_t place_offset,
568	        std::function<void(AggregateDataPtr &)> init,

578	        for (; i < size_unrolled; i += UNROLL_COUNT)
579	        {
580	            AggregateDataPtr places[UNROLL_COUNT];
581	            for (size_t j = 0; j < UNROLL_COUNT; ++j)
582	            {
583	                AggregateDataPtr & place = map[key[i + j]];
584	                if (unlikely(!place))
585	                    init(place);
586	
587	                places[j] = place;
588	            }

590	            for (size_t j = 0; j < UNROLL_COUNT; ++j)
591	                static_cast<const Derived *>(this)->add(places[j] + place_offset, columns, i + j, arena);
592	        }
593	
594	        for (; i < row_end; ++i)
595	        {
596	            AggregateDataPtr & place = map[key[i]];
597	            if (unlikely(!place))
598	                init(place);
599	            static_cast<const Derived *>(this)->add(place + place_offset, columns, i, arena);
600	        }

613	
614	        try
615	        {
616	            for (; batch_index < row_end; ++batch_index)
617	            {
618	                static_cast<const Derived *>(this)->insertResultInto(places[batch_index] + place_offset, to, arena);
619	
620	                if (destroy_place_after_insert)
621	                    static_cast<const Derived *>(this)->destroy(places[batch_index] + place_offset);
622	            }
623	        }
624	        catch (...)
625	        {

627	                static_cast<const Derived *>(this)->destroy(places[destroy_index] + place_offset);

629	            throw;

647	/// Implements several methods for manipulation with data. T - type of structure with data for aggregation.
648	template <typename T, typename Derived>
649	class IAggregateFunctionDataHelper : public IAggregateFunctionHelper<Derived>
650	{
651	protected:
652	    using Data = T;
653	
654	    static Data & data(AggregateDataPtr __restrict place) { return *reinterpret_cast<Data *>(place); }
655	    static const Data & data(ConstAggregateDataPtr __restrict place) { return *reinterpret_cast<const Data *>(place); }
656	
657	public:
658	    // Derived class can `override` this to flag that DateTime64 is not supported.
659	    static constexpr bool DateTime64Supported = true;
660	
661	    IAggregateFunctionDataHelper(const DataTypes & argument_types_, const Array & parameters_)
662	        : IAggregateFunctionHelper<Derived>(argument_types_, parameters_) {}
663	
664	    void create(AggregateDataPtr __restrict place) const override /// NOLINT
665	    {
666	        new (place) Data;
667	    }
668	
669	    void destroy(AggregateDataPtr __restrict place) const noexcept override
670	    {
671	        data(place).~Data();
672	    }
673	
674	    bool hasTrivialDestructor() const override
675	    {
676	        return std::is_trivially_destructible_v<Data>;
677	    }
678	
679	    size_t sizeOfData() const override
680	    {
681	        return sizeof(Data);
682	    }
683	
684	    size_t alignOfData() const override
685	    {
686	        return alignof(Data);
687	    }
688	
689	    void addBatchLookupTable8(
690	        size_t row_begin,
691	        size_t row_end,
692	        AggregateDataPtr * map,
693	        size_t place_offset,
694	        std::function<void(AggregateDataPtr &)> init,
695	        const UInt8 * key,
696	        const IColumn ** columns,
697	        Arena * arena) const override
698	    {
699	        const Derived & func = *static_cast<const Derived *>(this);
700	
701	        /// If the function is complex or too large, use more generic algorithm.
702	
703	        if (func.allocatesMemoryInArena() || sizeof(Data) > 16 || func.sizeOfData() != sizeof(Data))
704	        {
705	            IAggregateFunctionHelper<Derived>::addBatchLookupTable8(row_begin, row_end, map, place_offset, init, key, columns, arena);
706	            return;
707	        }
708	
709	        /// Will use UNROLL_COUNT number of lookup tables.
710	
711	        static constexpr size_t UNROLL_COUNT = 4;
712	
713	        std::unique_ptr<Data[]> places{new Data[256 * UNROLL_COUNT]};
714	        bool has_data[256 * UNROLL_COUNT]{}; /// Separate flags array to avoid heavy initialization.
715	
716	        size_t i = row_begin;
717	
718	        /// Aggregate data into different lookup tables.
719	
720	        size_t size_unrolled = (row_end - row_begin) / UNROLL_COUNT * UNROLL_COUNT;
721	        for (; i < size_unrolled; i += UNROLL_COUNT)
722	        {
723	            for (size_t j = 0; j < UNROLL_COUNT; ++j)
724	            {
725	                size_t idx = j * 256 + key[i + j];
726	                if (unlikely(!has_data[idx]))
727	                {
728	                    new (&places[idx]) Data;
729	                    has_data[idx] = true;
730	                }
731	                func.add(reinterpret_cast<char *>(&places[idx]), columns, i + j, nullptr);
732	            }
733	        }
734	
735	        /// Merge data from every lookup table to the final destination.
736	
737	        for (size_t k = 0; k < 256; ++k)
738	        {
739	            for (size_t j = 0; j < UNROLL_COUNT; ++j)
740	            {
741	                size_t idx = j * 256 + k;
742	                if (has_data[idx])
743	                {
744	                    AggregateDataPtr & place = map[k];
745	                    if (unlikely(!place))
746	                        init(place);
747	
748	                    func.merge(place + place_offset, reinterpret_cast<const char *>(&places[idx]), nullptr);
749	                }
750	            }
751	        }
752	
753	        /// Process tails and add directly to the final destination.
754	
755	        for (; i < row_end; ++i)
756	        {
757	            size_t k = key[i];
758	            AggregateDataPtr & place = map[k];
759	            if (unlikely(!place))
760	                init(place);
761	
762	            func.add(place + place_offset, columns, i, nullptr);
763	        }
764	    }
765	};

1	title: parseDataTimeBestEffort support comma between date and time
2	category: feature
3	requirement: '## Context
4

6	
7

10	  Teach `parseDateTimeBestEffort` to accept a comma between the date and time when the rest of the value is a complete date-time. Inputs that contain a comma but do not actually form a full timestamp should still fail with `Cannot read DateTime: unexpected word after Date` rather than being partially accepted.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  A value like a normal date-time with a comma separator parses successfully, while malformed inputs that only look similar continue to fail with the explicit parse error. The function becomes more tolerant without becoming ambiguous.

1	title: Fix a bug in ParserCreateUserQuery
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Administrators writing `CREATE USER` and related access-control statements expect host clauses and rename syntax to parse reliably, even under unusual input sequences found by fuzzing. A parser bug in this area turns valid account-management SQL into hard-to-diagnose syntax failures.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  The `CREATE USER` parser should accept the intended host-prefix forms without depending on a temporary C-string wrapper, and ALTER-style parsing should no longer carry dead state that can interfere with rename handling. This is a correctness fix for access-management SQL rather than a change in feature scope.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Previously failing edge cases around user host parsing and rename handling are parsed successfully, and the accepted SQL grammar for account-management statements behaves consistently instead of depending on fragile internal string handling.
16	
17	  '

1	title: Fix a bug in ParserFunction
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  SQL users expect the parser to finish building a function or tuple expression only after the parser layer has actually completed, especially around nested parentheses where a single element can mean either grouping or `tuple(...)`. The current parser bug can finalize too early and mis-handle valid expressions discovered by fuzzing.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Function-expression parsing should only yield a final AST after the parser layer is finished, while still preserving the special handling where round brackets with one non-tuple element remain that element and tuple syntax still becomes `tuple(...)` when appropriate. Valid queries should parse reliably instead of being dropped or misclassified by early result extraction.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Previously failing edge cases with nested function and bracket parsing are accepted, single grouped expressions are not accidentally rewritten into tuples, and tuple syntax continues to parse as `tuple(...)` only when the input really represents a tuple.
16	
17	  '

11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Those three function names are available in SQL, they accept U.S.-formatted timestamp input with `DateTime64` precision, and the `OrNull` and `OrZero` variants follow the expected fallback behavior instead of throwing on invalid input.
16	
17	  '

title: Fix logical error in right storage join with using
category: bugfix
requirement: '## Context

  Analysts joining against a `StorageJoin` table with `RIGHT JOIN ... USING (...)` expect either a correct result or an ordinary semantic error, not an internal logical error in the join machinery.


  ## Desired outcome

  Fix the right-join path so `StorageJoin` works correctly with `USING` in the affected scenario.


  ## Acceptance signals

  The targeted `RIGHT JOIN` queries execute normally and produce stable results instead of failing with an internal logical error.

  '
title: Set linker for RISC-V 64
category: other
requirement: '## Context

  Contributors building ClickHouse for `riscv64` need the cross-toolchain to pick a working linker automatically instead of failing at link time.

  ## Desired outcome

  The `riscv64` toolchain configuration should declare the expected linker so the build can complete without manual intervention.

  ## Acceptance signals

  `riscv64` builds use the configured linker successfully, with no runtime behavior changes.

  '
title: Change email for robot-clickhouse to immutable one
category: other
requirement: '## Context

  Release and CI automation should use a robot identity that remains stable over time, because generated commits and workflow actions need a durable attribution that does not change when a personal address does.


  ## Desired outcome

  Switch the affected automation to an immutable `robot-clickhouse` email identity without changing what the automation does.


  ## Acceptance signals

  The same release and CI steps still run as before, but new automated actions consistently carry the stable robot address.

  '
title: Add a limit for string size in RowBinary format
category: feature
requirement: '## Context

  Users reading `RowBinary` from untrusted or corrupted input need protection against absurd string lengths, because a bogus encoded size can otherwise force ClickHouse to attempt a huge memory allocation.


  ## Desired outcome

  Add a `RowBinary` string-size guard controlled by `format_binary_max_string_size`, with a default of `1GiB` and `0` meaning no limit, so oversized strings fail fast instead of exhausting memory.


  ## Acceptance signals

  `RowBinary` input that exceeds `format_binary_max_string_size` is rejected with `TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE`, normal inputs still load, and the new setting is documented as part of the `RowBinary` format contract.

  '
title: Fix preserving user configs in rpm packages
category: bugfix
requirement: '## Context

  Package upgrades should preserve local server, client, and Keeper configuration files that operators have customized. If the RPM spec treats those files like ordinary package payload, an upgrade can overwrite or discard important local settings.


  ## Desired outcome

  RPM packaging for the ClickHouse server, client, and Keeper should mark the shipped configuration files in a way that preserves user-modified configs during upgrades instead of replacing them silently. The operational requirement is safe package updates, not a change in database behavior.


  ## Acceptance signals

  Upgrading the RPM packages keeps existing local config edits intact for server, client, and Keeper installations, and package-managed defaults are handled as replacement candidates rather than overwriting the operator''s live configuration in place.

  '

  `pmod` should provide Spark-compatible non-negative results and its documentation should say so clearly enough that migration behavior is unsurprising.

  ## Acceptance signals

=== poco-config-performance ===
title: Update Poco
category: other
requirement: '## Context

  Operators with very large XML configurations still need configuration loading and key enumeration to stay usable after a dependency update, because startup and config inspection become impractical if repeated XML elements degrade badly.


  ## Desired outcome

  Keep the configuration stack efficient for extremely repetitive XML so a document with 1,000,000 repeated `<x><name>...</name></x>` elements still exposes keys like `x.name`, `x[1].name`, and the last indexed element correctly.


  ## Acceptance signals

  Loading and enumerating that large configuration remain within a reasonable bound, `configuration->keys("", keys)` returns all 1,000,000 entries, and indexed access keeps the expected `x`, `x[1]`, and final-element contract.

  '

1	title: 'Merging #36877'
2	category: other
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  An operator running replicated MergeTree mutations with non-deterministic expressions needs replicas to converge on byte-identical parts, even when a mutation result cannot safely be recomputed independently on every replica. Today a replica can try to rebuild the mutated part locally instead of fetching the committed result, which risks divergence for updates that use functions such as `hostName()`.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  When a mutation contains non-deterministic logic and replication requires an identical result, ClickHouse should fetch the merged part from the replica that first committed it rather than recalculating it locally. Operators should be able to run such mutations with `allow_nondeterministic_mutations = 1` and still end up with the same bytes on every replica.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  A replicated mutation like `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE z = hostName() WHERE 1 = 1` finishes with the same stored values on the follower replica as on the source replica, and the server log explains the fallback by saying `We will download merged part from replica to force byte-identical result.`. Existing deterministic mutation flows remain unchanged.'

8	/** Allows to randomize thread scheduling and insert various glitches across whole program for testing purposes.
9	  * It is done by setting up a timer that will send PROF signal to every thread when certain amount of CPU time has passed.
10	  *
11	  * To initialize ThreadFuzzer, call ThreadFuzzer::instance().
12	  * The behaviour is controlled by environment variables:
13	  *
14	  * THREAD_FUZZER_CPU_TIME_PERIOD_US  - period of signals in microseconds.
15	  * THREAD_FUZZER_YIELD_PROBABILITY   - probability to do 'sched_yield'.
16	  * THREAD_FUZZER_MIGRATE_PROBABILITY - probability to set CPU affinity to random CPU core.
17	  * THREAD_FUZZER_SLEEP_PROBABILITY   - probability to sleep.
18	  * THREAD_FUZZER_SLEEP_TIME_US       - amount of time to sleep in microseconds.
19	  *
20	  * ThreadFuzzer will do nothing if environment variables are not set accordingly.
21	  *
22	  * The intention is to reproduce thread synchronization bugs (race conditions and deadlocks) more frequently in tests.
23	  * We already have tests with TSan. But TSan only covers "physical" synchronization bugs, but not "logical" ones,
24	  *  where all data is protected by synchronization primitives, but we still have race conditions.
25	  * Obviously, TSan cannot debug distributed synchronization bugs.
26	  *
27	  * The motivation for this tool is an evidence, that concurrency bugs are more likely to reproduce
28	  *  on bad unstable virtual machines in a dirty environments.
29	  *
30	  * The idea is not new, see also:
31	  * https://channel9.msdn.com/blogs/peli/concurrency-fuzzing-with-cuzz
32	  *
33	  * Notes:
34	  * - it can be also implemented with instrumentation (example: LLVM Xray) instead of signals.
35	  * - we should also make the sleep time random.
36	  * - sleep and migration obviously helps, but the effect of yield is unclear.
37	  *
38	  * In addition, we allow to inject glitches around thread synchronization functions.
39	  * Example:
40	  *
41	  * THREAD_FUZZER_pthread_mutex_lock_BEFORE_SLEEP_PROBABILITY=0.001
42	  * THREAD_FUZZER_pthread_mutex_lock_BEFORE_SLEEP_TIME_US=10000
43	  * THREAD_FUZZER_pthread_mutex_lock_AFTER_SLEEP_PROBABILITY=0.001
44	  * THREAD_FUZZER_pthread_mutex_lock_AFTER_SLEEP_TIME_US=10000
45	  */

352	{
353	    /// There was an AVX here but with mash with SSE instructions, we got a big slowdown.
354	#if defined(__SSE2__)

358	        _mm_loadu_si128(reinterpret_cast<const __m128i *>(src + 16)));

365	inline void wildCopy32(UInt8 * dst, const UInt8 * src, const UInt8 * dst_end)
366	{
367	    /// Unrolling with clang is doing >10% performance degrade.
368	#if defined(__clang__)
369	    #pragma nounroll
370	#endif
371	    do
372	    {
373	        copy32(dst, src);
374	        dst += 32;
375	        src += 32;
376	    } while (dst < dst_end);

473	
474	template <size_t copy_amount, bool use_shuffle>
475	bool NO_INLINE decompressImpl(
476	     const char * const source,
477	     char * const dest,
478	     size_t source_size,
479	     size_t dest_size)
480	{
481	    const UInt8 * ip = reinterpret_cast<const UInt8 *>(source);
482	    UInt8 * op = reinterpret_cast<UInt8 *>(dest);
483	    const UInt8 * const input_end = ip + source_size;
484	    UInt8 * const output_begin = op;
485	    UInt8 * const output_end = op + dest_size;
486	
487	    /// Unrolling with clang is doing >10% performance degrade.
488	#if defined(__clang__)
489	    #pragma nounroll
490	#endif
491	    while (true)
492	    {
493	        size_t length;
494	
495	        auto continue_read_length = [&]
496	        {
497	            unsigned s;
498	            do
499	            {
500	                s = *ip++;
501	                length += s;
502	            } while (unlikely(s == 255 && ip < input_end));
503	        };
504	
505	        /// Get literal length.
506	
507	        if (unlikely(ip >= input_end))
508	            return false;
509	
510	        const unsigned token = *ip++;
511	        length = token >> 4;
512	        if (length == 0x0F)
513	        {
514	            if (unlikely(ip + 1 >= input_end))
515	                return false;
516	            continue_read_length();
517	        }
518	
519	        /// Copy literals.
520	
521	        UInt8 * copy_end = op + length;
522	
523	        /// input: Hello, world
524	        ///        ^-ip
525	        /// output: xyz
526	        ///            ^-op  ^-copy_end
527	        /// output: xyzHello, w
528	        ///                   ^- excessive copied bytes due to "wildCopy"
529	        /// input: Hello, world
530	        ///              ^-ip
531	        /// output: xyzHello, w
532	        ///                  ^-op (we will overwrite excessive bytes on next iteration)
533	
534	        if (unlikely(copy_end > output_end))
535	            return false;
536	
537	        // Due to implementation specifics the copy length is always a multiple of copy_amount
538	        size_t real_length = 0;
539	
540	        static_assert(copy_amount == 8 || copy_amount == 16 || copy_amount == 32);
541	        if constexpr (copy_amount == 8)
542	            real_length = (((length >> 3) + 1) * 8);
543	        else if constexpr (copy_amount == 16)
544	            real_length = (((length >> 4) + 1) * 16);
545	        else if constexpr (copy_amount == 32)
546	            real_length = (((length >> 5) + 1) * 32);
547	
548	        if (unlikely(ip + real_length >= input_end + ADDITIONAL_BYTES_AT_END_OF_BUFFER))
549	             return false;
550	
551	        wildCopy<copy_amount>(op, ip, copy_end);    /// Here we can write up to copy_amount - 1 bytes after buffer.
552	
553	        if (copy_end == output_end)
554	            return true;
555	
556	        ip += length;
557	        op = copy_end;
558	
559	        if (unlikely(ip + 1 >= input_end))
560	            return false;
561	
562	        /// Get match offset.
563	
564	        size_t offset = unalignedLoad<UInt16>(ip);
565	        ip += 2;
566	        const UInt8 * match = op - offset;
567	
568	        if (unlikely(match < output_begin))
569	            return false;
570	
571	        /// Get match length.
572	
573	        length = token & 0x0F;
574	        if (length == 0x0F)
575	        {
576	            if (unlikely(ip + 1 >= input_end))
577	                return false;
578	            continue_read_length();
579	        }
580	        length += 4;
581	
582	        /// Copy match within block, that produce overlapping pattern. Match may replicate itself.
583	
584	        copy_end = op + length;
585	
586	        /** Here we can write up to copy_amount - 1 - 4 * 2 bytes after buffer.
587	          * The worst case when offset = 1 and length = 4
588	          */
589	
590	        if (unlikely(offset < copy_amount))
591	        {
592	            /// output: Hello
593	            ///              ^-op
594	            ///         ^-match; offset = 5
595	            ///
596	            /// output: Hello
597	            ///         [------] - copy_amount bytes
598	            ///              [------] - copy them here
599	            ///
600	            /// output: HelloHelloHel
601	            ///            ^-match   ^-op

603	            copyOverlap<copy_amount, use_shuffle>(op, match, offset);

633	    PerformanceStatistics & statistics [[maybe_unused]])

649	        /// Run the selected method and measure time.
650	
651	        Stopwatch watch;
652	        bool success = true;
653	        if (best_variant == 0)
654	            success = decompressImpl<16, true>(source, dest, source_size, dest_size);

663	
664	        watch.stop();
665

667	
668	        statistics.data[best_variant].update(watch.elapsedSeconds(), dest_size);
669	
670	        return success;

3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  A ClickHouse operator shutting down a server that uses distributed DDL should not hit shutdown-time races between `DDLWorker` and ZooKeeper cleanup.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Server shutdown should destroy `DDLWorker` before ZooKeeper teardown so the worker cannot revive or touch ZooKeeper while the shutdown sequence is already in progress.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  Shutdown completes without the old race between `DDLWorker` and ZooKeeper, and distributed DDL behavior during normal operation is unchanged.
16	
17	  '

1	title: Add support for SHOW FULL
2	category: feature
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Analysts and tooling that use MySQL-style introspection expect `SHOW FULL` to be accepted when listing objects, because the modifier is commonly used to distinguish plain tables from views and other table-like objects.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  Add `SHOW FULL` support so `SHOW FULL TABLES` is parsed and returns the richer object-kind information instead of rejecting the modifier.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  `SHOW FULL` is accepted by the parser and interpreter, and the result distinguishes object types in a way that ordinary `SHOW TABLES` does not.
16	
17	  '

From dd8478422a4d6c76b421569588efda00bee2022a Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Azat Khuzhin <a3at.mail@gmail.com>
Date: Fri, 2 Sep 2022 14:15:18 +0200
Subject: [PATCH] Fix usage of generator expressions for libcxx cmake

Before, if you store clickhouse sources in /src, there was a typo and it
produce the following error:

    CMake Error in contrib/libcxx-cmake/CMakeLists.txt:
      Target "cxx" INTERFACE_INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES property contains path:

        "/src"

      which is prefixed in the source directory.

Also move "src" into PRIVATE, since it is required only for libcxx
itself.

Signed-off-by: Azat Khuzhin <a.khuzhin@semrush.com>
---
 contrib/libcxx-cmake/CMakeLists.txt | 5 ++---
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 3 deletions(-)

diff --git a/contrib/libcxx-cmake/CMakeLists.txt b/contrib/libcxx-cmake/CMakeLists.txt
index a501c4df64fb..6f42a4795881 100644
--- a/contrib/libcxx-cmake/CMakeLists.txt
+++ b/contrib/libcxx-cmake/CMakeLists.txt
@@ -54,9 +54,8 @@ set(SRCS
 add_library(cxx ${SRCS})
 set_target_properties(cxx PROPERTIES FOLDER "contrib/libcxx-cmake")
 
-target_include_directories(cxx SYSTEM BEFORE PUBLIC
-        $<BUILD_INTERFACE:${LIBCXX_SOURCE_DIR}/include>
-        $<BUILD_INTERFACE:${LIBCXX_SOURCE_DIR}>/src)
+target_include_directories(cxx SYSTEM BEFORE PRIVATE $<BUILD_INTERFACE:${LIBCXX_SOURCE_DIR}/src>)
+target_include_directories(cxx SYSTEM BEFORE PUBLIC  $<BUILD_INTERFACE:${LIBCXX_SOURCE_DIR}/include>)
 target_compile_definitions(cxx PRIVATE -D_LIBCPP_BUILDING_LIBRARY -DLIBCXX_BUILDING_LIBCXXABI)
 
 # Enable capturing stack traces for all exceptions.

1	title: Fix the race between waitMutation and updating local queue from ZK
2	category: bugfix
3	requirement: '## Context
4	
5	  Operators waiting on a mutation in a replicated MergeTree table expect `waitMutation` to reflect the local replica’s real state, even while ZooKeeper updates are still arriving. A race in replica ordering can make the wait path report that a mutation was killed or unfinished when the local queue simply has not been checked first.
6	
7	
8	  ## Desired outcome
9	
10	  The local replica should be prioritized when evaluating mutation completion so `waitMutation` does not lose to a timing race with queue refreshes from ZooKeeper.
11	
12	
13	  ## Acceptance signals
14	
15	  A mutation that has completed locally no longer intermittently reports an `UNFINISHED` or killed-style outcome because another replica was examined first, and waiting behavior is stable under ordinary replication lag.
16	
17	  '

+# 安全更新日志
+## 修复于ClickHouse 22.9.1.2603, 2022-09-22
+### CVE-2022-44011
+ClickHouse server中发现了一个堆缓冲区溢出问题。拥有向ClickHouse Server导入数据能力的恶意用户，可通过插入畸形CapnProto对象使ClickHouse Server对象崩溃。
+
+修复已推送至版本22.9.1.2603, 22.8.2.11，22.7.4.16，22.6.6.16，22.3.12.19
+
+作者：Kiojj(独立研究者)
+
+### CVE-2022-44010
+ClickHouse server中发现了一个堆缓冲区溢出问题。攻击者可发送一个特殊的HTTP请求至HTTP端口（默认监听在8123端口），该攻击可造成堆缓冲区溢出进而使ClickHouse server进程崩溃。执行该攻击无需认证。
+
+修复版本已推送至版本22.9.1.2603，22.8.2.11，22.7.4.16，22.6.6.16，22.3.12.19
+
+作者：Kiojj(独立研究者)
+
+## 修复于ClickHouse 21.10.2.15，2021-10-18
+### CVE-2021-43304
+在对恶意查询做语法分析时，ClickHouse的LZ4压缩编码会堆缓冲区溢出。LZ4:decompressImpl循环尤其是wildCopy<copy_amount>(op, ip, copy_end)中的随意复制操作没有验证是否会导致超出目标缓冲区限制。
+
+作者：JFrog 安全研究团队
+
+### CVE-2021-43305
+在对恶意查询做语法分析时，ClickHouse的LZ4压缩编码会堆缓冲区溢出。LZ4:decompressImpl循环尤其是wildCopy<copy_amount>(op, ip, copy_end)中的随意复制操作没有验证是否会导致超出目标缓冲区限制。
+该问题于CVE-2021-43304非常相似，但是无保护的copy操作存在于不同的wildCopy调用里。
+
+作者：JFrog 安全研究团队
+
+### CVE-2021-42387
+在对恶意查询做语法分析时，ClickHouse的LZ4:decompressImpl循环会从压缩数据中读取一个用户提供的16bit无符号值（'offset'）。这个offset后面在复制操作作为长度使用时，没有检查是否超过复制源的上限。
+
+作者：JFrog 安全研究团队
+
+### CVE-2021-42388
+在对恶意查询做语法分析时，ClickHouse的LZ4:decompressImpl循环会从压缩数据中读取一个用户提供的16bit无符号值（'offset'）。这个offset后面在复制操作作为长度使用时，没有检查是否越过复制源的下限。
+
+作者：JFrog 安全研究团队
+
+### CVE-2021-42389
+在对恶意查询做语法分析时，ClickHouse的Delta压缩编码存在除零错误。压缩缓存的首字节在取模时没有判断是否为0。
+
+作者：JFrog 安全研究团队
+
+### CVE-2021-42390
+在对恶意查询做语法分析时，ClickHouse的DeltaDouble压缩编码存在除零错误。压缩缓存的首字节在取模时没有判断是否为0。
+
+作者：JFrog 安全研究团队
+
+### CVE-2021-42391
+在对恶意查询做语法分析时，  ClickHouse的Gorilla压缩编码存在除零错误，压缩缓存的首字节取模时没有判断是否为0。
+
+作者：JFrog 安全研究团队
+
+## 修复于ClickHouse 21.4.3.21，2021-04-12
+### CVE-2021-25263
+拥有CREATE DICTIONARY权限的攻击者，可以读取许可目录之外的任意文件。
+
+修复已推送至版本20.8.18.32-lts，21.1.9.41-stable，21.2.9.41-stable，21.3.6.55-lts，21.4.3.21-stable以及更早期的版本。
+
+作者：[Vyacheslav Egoshin](https://twitter.com/vegoshin)

56	    /// Check if table function needs a structure hint from SELECT query in case of

59	    virtual bool needStructureHint() const { return false; }
60	
61	    /// Set a structure hint from SELECT query in case of
62	    /// INSERT INTO FUNCTION ... SELECT ...
63	    /// This hint could be used not to repeat schema in function arguments.
64	    virtual void setStructureHint(const ColumnsDescription &) {}
65	
66	    /// Create storage according to the query.
67	    StoragePtr
68	    execute(const ASTPtr & ast_function, ContextPtr context, const std::string & table_name, ColumnsDescription cached_columns_ = {}, bool use_global_context = false) const;
69	
70	    virtual ~ITableFunction() = default;
71

---
sidebar_position: 25
sidebar_label: MySQL Interface
---

# MySQL Interface

ClickHouse supports the MySQL wire protocol. This allows certain clients that do not have ClickHouse connectors leverage the MySQL protocol instead, and it has been validated with the following BI tools:

- [Looker Studio](../integrations/data-visualization/looker-studio-and-clickhouse.md)
- [Tableau Online](../integrations/tableau-online)
- [QuickSight](../integrations/quicksight)

If you are trying other untested clients or integrations, keep in mind that there could be the following limitations:

- SSL implementation might not be fully compatible; there could be potential [TLS SNI](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/ssl/what-is-sni/) issues.
- A particular tool might require dialect features (e.g., MySQL-specific functions or settings) that are not implemented yet.

If there is a native driver available (e.g., [DBeaver](../integrations/dbeaver)), it is always preferred to use it instead of the MySQL interface. Additionally, while most of the MySQL language clients should work fine, MySQL interface is not guaranteed to be a drop-in replacement for a codebase with existing MySQL queries.

If your use case involves a particular tool that does not have a native ClickHouse driver, and you want to use it via MySQL interface, and you found certain compatibility issues - please [create an issue](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues) in the ClickHouse repository.

## Enabling the MySQL Interface

Add the [mysql_port](../../operations/server-configuration-parameters/settings.md#server_configuration_parameters-mysql_port) setting to your server's configuration file. For example, you could define the port in a new XML file in your `config.d/` folder:

```xml
<clickhouse>
    <mysql_port>9004</mysql_port>
</clickhouse>
```

Startup your ClickHouse server and look for a log message similar to the following that mentions Listening for MySQL compatibility protocol:

```bash
{} <Information> Application: Listening for MySQL compatibility protocol: 127.0.0.1:9004
```

## Connect MySQL to ClickHouse

The following command demonstrates how to connect the MySQL client `mysql` to ClickHouse:

```bash
mysql --protocol tcp -h localhost -u default -P 9004
```

Output if a connection succeeded:

```text
Welcome to the MySQL monitor.  Commands end with ; or \g.
Your MySQL connection id is 4
Server version: 22.11.2.30-ClickHouse

Copyright (c) 2000, 2022, Oracle and/or its affiliates.

Oracle is a registered trademark of Oracle Corporation and/or its
affiliates. Other names may be trademarks of their respective
owners.

Type 'help;' or '\h' for help. Type '\c' to clear the current input statement.

mysql>
```

For compatibility with all MySQL clients, it is recommended to specify user password with [double SHA1](../../operations/settings/settings-users.md#user-namepassword) in the configuration file.
If user password is specified using [SHA256](../../sql-reference/functions/hash-functions.md#hash_functions-sha256), some clients won't be able to authenticate (mysqljs and old versions of command-line tool `mysql`).

Restrictions:

- prepared queries are not supported

- some data types are sent as strings

To cancel a long query use `KILL QUERY connection_id` statement (it is replaced with `KILL QUERY WHERE query_id = connection_id` while proceeding). For example:

```bash
$ mysql --protocol tcp -h mysql_server -u default -P 9004 -e "KILL QUERY 123456;"
```

# 2022 Changelog

### ClickHouse release v22.7.2.15-stable FIXME as compared to v22.7.1.2484-stable

#### Bug Fix
* Backported in [#39750](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/39750): Fix seeking while reading from encrypted disk. This PR fixes [#38381](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/38381). [#39687](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/39687) ([Vitaly Baranov](https://github.com/vitlibar)).

#### Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in official stable or prestable release)

* Backported in [#39591](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/39591): Fix data race and possible heap-buffer-overflow in Avro format. Closes [#39094](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/39094) Closes [#33652](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/33652). [#39498](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/39498) ([Kruglov Pavel](https://github.com/Avogar)).
* Backported in [#39613](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/39613): Fix bug with maxsplit argument for splitByChar, which was not working correctly. [#39552](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/39552) ([filimonov](https://github.com/filimonov)).
* Backported in [#39792](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/39792): Fix wrong index analysis with tuples and operator `IN`, which could lead to wrong query result. [#39752](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/39752) ([Anton Popov](https://github.com/CurtizJ)).
* Backported in [#39837](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/39837): Fix `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA` exception with `local_filesystem_read_method=pread_threadpool`. This bug affected only Linux kernel version 5.9 and 5.10 according to [man](https://manpages.debian.org/testing/manpages-dev/preadv2.2.en.html#BUGS). [#39800](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/39800) ([Anton Popov](https://github.com/CurtizJ)).

#### NOT FOR CHANGELOG / INSIGNIFICANT

* Replace MemoryTrackerBlockerInThread to LockMemoryExceptionInThread [#39619](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/39619) ([Nikolai Kochetov](https://github.com/KochetovNicolai)).
* Change mysql-odbc url [#39702](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/39702) ([Mikhail f. Shiryaev](https://github.com/Felixoid)).

14	
15	  '

==> memory-accounting-rollback.yaml <==
title: Fix memory accounting in case of MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED errors
category: bugfix
requirement: '## Context

  Operators whose queries hit `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` can be left with memory still counted against the thread or query after the failed allocation path, which makes later activity look larger than it really is.

  ## Desired outcome

  Memory accounting should roll back correctly whenever an allocation fails with `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`.

  ## Acceptance signals

  After a limit-exceeded error, tracked memory returns to the proper value and subsequent queries start from clean accounting.

  '

==> revert-rss-memory-counter.yaml <==
title: Revert "Use separate counter for RSS in global memory tracker."
category: other
requirement: '## Context

  Operators watching memory limits during HTTP inserts with parallel parsing need the global memory tracker and `MemoryTracking` metric to reflect one consistent notion of total memory, but the separate RSS path introduces drift and misleading limit behavior.

  ## Desired outcome

  Total memory tracking should return to a single corrected source of truth so inserts either succeed normally or fail through the ordinary `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` path.

  ## Acceptance signals

  `MemoryTracking` reports the corrected total again, HTTP parallel parsing no longer misaccounts total memory, and limit errors use the normal `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` semantics rather than a special RSS-specific branch.

  '
